cues.text: A Gifted Dominican Scholar
Born at Valencia in 1350 to a family ennobled during the Christian reconquest of the city, Vincent entered the Dominican Order in 1367.
He quickly distinguished himself academically, teaching philosophy at Lérida by his early twenties and later theology at Barcelona.
He developed a formidable reputation as both scholar and preacher.
Preacher of Penance
After a severe illness and vision in 1398, Vincent became convinced he was specifically called to herald penance and prepare souls for judgment.
For the following two decades, he traveled almost ceaselessly across Spain, France, Italy, Switzerland, and the British Isles, preaching outdoors to enormous crowds.
He slept on the bare floor and lived in continual austerity, even as his fame as a wonder-worker and eloquent preacher spread across Western Christendom.
Caught in the Western Schism
Vincent's life was deeply entangled in the Western Schism , which had split papal allegiance since 1378.
Initially a supporter and close counselor of the Avignon claimant Benedict XIII, whom he had known personally, Vincent worked for years to persuade Benedict to resign.
He did so for the sake of Church unity, eventually concluding, after repeated refusals, that the schism could only be healed by withdrawing political support from Benedict XIII.
Helping End the Schism
Vincent's eventual counsel to King Ferdinand of Aragon to withdraw his allegiance from Benedict XIII helped weaken Benedict XIII's remaining political support.
It was one factor among several in the eventual resolution of the nearly forty-year schism in 1417 with the election of Pope Martin V.
Vincent lived to see this outcome before his own death two years later.
A Complicated Missionary Legacy
Vincent's preaching also produced large-scale conversions among Spain's Jewish population.
Historians have long debated how much reflected genuine persuasion versus coercive pressure from a hostile social and legal climate.
That climate made conversion increasingly difficult to refuse—a complex, troubling dimension of his broader missionary career that later scholarship has examined with considerable care.
Legacy
Vincent died at Vannes, in Brittany, on 5 April 1419, during a final preaching mission through northern France, and was canonized in 1455 by Pope Calixtus III.

He remains remembered above all as one of the medieval Church's most extraordinary popular preachers, and as a rare instance of a single figure whose personal counsel helped bring a decades-long papal schism to its close.
